descriptionChirho: To die, cease living — the basic intransitive Qal sense covering natural death, death by plague/famine, death in battle, and general mortality; Arabic مَاتَ/يَمُوتُ, Korean 죽다, Swahili -fa.

The dead, a dead person, corpse — Qal participle used as a substantive noun referring to a deceased person or corpse, often with possessive suffixes (my dead, your dead, his dead) or in prepositional phrases (among the dead, like the dead, for the dead); Arabic مَيِّتٌ/مَيِّتينَ, Korean 죽은 자, Swahili maiti/wafu.

Death as an abstract noun or event — Qal infinitive construct used nominally to denote the event or state of dying (my death, her dying, our dying, at the death of, to death); Arabic مَوْت, Korean 죽음, Swahili kufa/mauti.

The emphatic death-penalty formula מוֹת יוּמָת (dying he shall die / he shall surely die) — Qal infinitive absolute used adverbially to intensify the finite verb, typically in legal pronouncements prescribing capital punishment or divine warnings of certain death; Arabic مَوْتًا يَمُوتُ, Korean 반드시 죽으리라, Swahili hakika atakufa.
To be put to death, be executed — Hofal (passive of Hifil) expressing judicial or communal execution, frequently in legal codes; Arabic يُقْتَلُ/يُمَاتُ, Korean 죽임을 당하다, Swahili -uawa.

To kill, put to death, cause to die — Hifil causative covering intentional killing (murder, war, execution by an agent), with various subjects and objects; Arabic أَمَاتَ/قَتَلَ, Korean 죽이다, Swahili -ua.
To kill, slay — Piel/Polel intensive stem denoting repeated, vigorous, or emphatic killing; semantically close to Hifil but with intensive force; Arabic أَمَاتَ/يُمِيتُ, Korean 죽이다, Swahili -ua.
